overview: Temujin’s recognition as Chinggis Khan in 1206 joined steppe peoples under a new imperial leadership. Mongol conquests and later regional khanates reshaped much of Eurasia. This atlas’s supplied shapes show only Mongolia and eastern territories, not the full western conquests. Its 1294 endpoint marks Khubilai’s death; imperial authority had already fractured decades earlier.

periods.summary: Ögödei ruled from 1229; armies defeated the Jin and expanded far west.

periods.title: Imperial courts and contested succession
periods.summary: A wide empire connected mobile courts, cities and displaced populations.

periods.title: Rival branches of the ruling family
periods.summary: Civil wars and separate regional interests weakened common authority.

periods.title: Regional khanates and later legacies
periods.summary: Khubilai’s death did not end all Mongol governments or communities.

items.text: In 1206 an assembly of Mongol nobles recognized Temujin as Chinggis Khan. Alliances and the defeat of rivals had brought different groups under his leadership. The event is conventionally used to mark the empire’s beginning, rather than the beginning of Mongol people or their pastoral way of life.

Army organization used units of ten, a hundred, a thousand and ten thousand. This helped commanders coordinate people from different backgrounds. A feigned retreat could lure opponents into an ambush: soldiers appeared to flee while other forces waited. Such manoeuvres required discipline and communication, not simply fast horses.

Chinggis’s invasion of Central Asia began in 1219 and devastated major centres. Accounts describe mass killing, and conquest brought captivity and displacement as well as new connections. Remembering the merchants and ideas that later travelled across Mongol territories should not erase what the campaigns cost the people who already lived there.

Under Ögödei, who ruled from 1229 to 1241, Mongol armies defeated the Jin dynasty in northern China in 1234 and advanced into Rus’ and the Caucasus. Expansion involved many commanders and successive campaigns. The empire’s enormous reach belonged to generations of rulers, not to one man riding everywhere himself.

From around 1260, disputes over leadership increasingly divided the dynasty. Regional centres developed in China and Mongolia, Central Asia, Iran and the lands of the Golden Horde. Some branches fought each other over routes and grazing grounds. A shared ruling family did not guarantee a shared policy.

sections.title: Moving house, caring for animals and preparing food

items.text: Travelling in the 1250s, William of Rubruck described dwellings with circular wooden frames and felt covers, decorated with birds, animals and plants. Some large homes travelled on ox-drawn carts. These were portable households with belongings and carefully arranged interiors: moving house could mean taking the house along.

Rubruck described women driving carts, sewing clothing and working with cow’s milk, while men made saddles and bows and tended horses. Both women and men cared for sheep and goats. His account reveals many skilled jobs needed to keep a travelling household going.

For winter supplies, Rubruck described butter and dried sour curds made from cow’s milk. Hard curds could later be mixed with water. Preserving milk helped bridge seasonal shortages. This was food planning with herds, heat and sunshine, long before a kitchen refrigerator.

Rubruck also observed people letting water trickle from their mouths onto their hands or hair when washing. It is a specific medieval traveller’s report, not a rule for every Mongol household. Small descriptions like this give historians glimpses of personal care otherwise missing from royal chronicles.

Sheep provided meat, skins and wool that could be pressed into felt for clothes and shelter. Dried dung supplied fuel where wood was scarce; women and children gathered it. Helping a ewe accept and nurse her lamb could protect a family’s future supplies. Caring for animals was skilled, essential work.

Karakorum also had permanent workshops and buildings. Excavations in its craftsmen’s quarter found evidence of production, while nearby kilns made building materials. Bone working and vessel repair could serve ordinary customers as well as the court. The capital needed people who fixed useful things, alongside those who made impressive ones.

Chinese glazed bowls and other tableware reached Karakorum over long distances. Archaeology confirms the imported objects, while texts describe craftspeople brought from conquered regions, often as captives. The city’s mix of skills and cultures grew through both opportunity and coercion; not every person who made the capital remarkable had chosen to come.

A network of relay stations, called the yam, linked Karakorum with distant territories. Messages, embassies and merchants used these routes, and supplies also sustained a city that struggled to grow enough grain nearby. Communications and food transport helped turn widely separated courts and settlements into parts of an imperial system.

A surviving late-thirteenth-century Yuan travel pass is iron with silver filling its cut-out letters. Its Mongolian text uses the Phakpa script and invokes “the strength of Eternal Heaven”. This object identified imperial authority in a world of long journeys. The reverse lettering is inverted, an unusual detail left by its construction.

sections.title: A short piece of imperial writing

items.text: Güyük’s 1246 letter to Pope Innocent IV carries a Mongolian seal. Part of its inscription reads “yeke Mongγol ulus-un”, translated by Igor de Rachewiltz as “of the Great Mongol Nation”. This is a scholarly Roman transcription of the vertical Uyghur-Mongolian script. The words show how imperial authority was named in an actual diplomatic document.

ending.text: The empire divided through succession wars and the growth of regional khanates, especially from the 1260s onward. Khubilai’s death in 1294 was not a single collapse of all Mongol rule. Yuan, Ilkhanid, Golden Horde and Central Asian governments followed different political histories; Mongol communities continued beyond them. The atlas’s eastern shapes and endpoint cannot show that whole, uneven process.
